html:
A league of merchant towns in northern Germany and around the Baltic that ruled trade in the Baltic and North Sea from the 1200s to the 1400s. It is often dated from its first general diet, at Lübeck in 1356; its last diet met in 1669.

It grew out of groups of German merchants who travelled together for safety. Led by Lübeck, it included Hamburg, Bremen, Cologne, Danzig, Riga and, at its height, some 200 towns. It had trading posts in Bruges, London, Bergen and Novgorod. Its sturdy ships, called cogs, carried:

  • grain, timber, furs, wax and amber from the east;
  • herring and dried cod from Scania and Norway;
  • cloth from Flanders and England, and salt and wine from the west.

The Hansa had no state of its own but could wage war. After beating Denmark, it won the Peace of Stralsund in 1370, which gave it control of the Sound. It declined from the 1400s as Dutch and English shipping grew and strong states such as Muscovy and Poland and Lithuania rose. In the south, merchants met at the Champagne fairs and in Venice.
